back: Peered virtual networks must not overlap; the remedy is renumbering. Keyword: plan addresses before deploying.
Network, broadcast, and three platform addresses. A /29 yields three usable, and /29 is the smallest allowed. Keyword: subtract five.
GatewaySubnet, AzureFirewallSubnet, AzureBastionSubnet, RouteServerSubnet — exact names, minimum sizes, nothing else in them. Keyword: reserved names.
Hands a subnet to a platform service so it can inject its own resources. Keyword: the service owns it.
Standard is zone-redundant, secure by default with no inbound unless permitted, and required by Standard Load Balancer. Keyword: design on Standard.
The Azure-provided DNS resolver; a custom DNS server forwards here to resolve Azure names. Keyword: the magic address.
A zone must be linked to a virtual network to be used there; auto-registration adds machine records. Keyword: link or it does nothing.
Inbound endpoints for on-premises to query Azure zones, outbound plus rulesets for Azure to resolve on-premises. Replaces DNS VMs. Keyword: hybrid resolution.
A peered to B and B to C does not let A reach C. Fix with mesh, hub-and-spoke plus UDRs, or Virtual WAN. Keyword: no transit.
Spokes use the hub's VPN or ExpressRoute gateway; needs allow-forwarded-traffic and use-remote-gateways set on the right sides. Keyword: both sides.
Longest prefix match first; on a tie, user-defined route beats BGP beats system. Keyword: UDR wins ties.
A 0.0.0.0/0 user-defined route sending internet-bound traffic to a gateway or appliance for inspection. Keyword: default route.
The recommended outbound option; scales SNAT ports far beyond a load balancer and takes precedence on its subnet. Keyword: SNAT exhaustion.

front: Route Server is control plane only
back: Exchanges BGP routes with an appliance and programs them into the VNet. It never carries data traffic. Keyword: routes, not packets.
Route-based for multiple tunnels, ExpressRoute coexistence, point-to-site, and IKEv2. Policy-based is one tunnel, IKEv1, legacy only. Keyword: route-based by default.
Both instances carry traffic with two public IPs and two tunnels, removing the failover interruption of active-standby. Keyword: no failover gap.
Represents the on-premises endpoint and its address space — the Azure object describing the far side. Keyword: the other end.
Microsoft Entra ID authentication for point-to-site requires the OpenVPN tunnel type. Keyword: the pairing.
Windows-only, TLS-based, so it traverses firewalls that block UDP. Keyword: TLS through restrictive firewalls.
Must be regenerated whenever the point-to-site configuration changes; a stale package is why clients stop connecting. Keyword: regenerate.
Private peering reaches virtual networks; Microsoft peering reaches Microsoft public services such as Microsoft 365. Keyword: private vs public services.
Connects two ExpressRoute circuits so on-premises sites reach each other over Microsoft's backbone. Keyword: site to site via Microsoft.
Sends data traffic straight to virtual machines, bypassing the ExpressRoute gateway. The gateway is still needed for routing. Keyword: bypass for data only.
Add IPsec — a VPN over private peering, or MACsec on ExpressRoute Direct. Keyword: private ≠ encrypted.
Basic is site-to-site VPN only. Standard adds ExpressRoute, point-to-site, and hub-to-hub transit. Keyword: Standard for anything real.
A Virtual WAN hub with Azure Firewall in it; routing intent directs traffic through inspection without per-spoke UDRs. Keyword: inspection in the hub.
TCP and UDP within a region; it cannot route by URL path or host name. Keyword: no HTTP awareness.
Secure by default with no implicit outbound access — outbound rules or NAT Gateway must be configured. Keyword: no free outbound.
A global anycast IP above regional load balancers, with automatic regional failover. Keyword: one IP, many regions.
It returns a different answer per routing method and is not in the data path, so failover depends on DNS TTL. Keyword: DNS, not proxy.
Routes by host name so one Application Gateway serves several sites. Keyword: host-based.
Sends different URL paths to different backend pools — an images path and an API path on one gateway. Keyword: layer 7 only.
Termination decrypts at the gateway to inspect and route; end-to-end re-encrypts to the backend. Keyword: does it stay encrypted.
Far more often a health probe path or NSG problem than a broken application. Keyword: check the probe first.

front: Locking down a Front Door origin
back: Restrict to the AzureFrontDoor.Backend service tag and validate X-Azure-FDID, or use Private Link on Premium. Keyword: don't let traffic bypass the WAF.
One endpoint maps to one instance and one sub-resource; blob and file need two. Keyword: one per sub-resource.
Reachable from peered networks and from on-premises over VPN or ExpressRoute — unlike service endpoints. Keyword: works from on-premises.

front: Reachable by IP, not by name
back: A DNS problem every time — the public host name must resolve to the private IP via the linked private DNS zone. Keyword: DNS.
Publishes your own service behind a Standard internal load balancer for consumers to reach via their own private endpoints. Keyword: you are the provider.

front: Service endpoint keeps the public path
back: Traffic still reaches the service's public endpoint and the resource keeps a public IP. Keyword: not private.
Restricts which specific resources a subnet may reach over a service endpoint — stops exfiltration to a foreign storage account. Keyword: narrow the target.
They do not extend beyond the virtual network, so hybrid access to PaaS needs a private endpoint. Keyword: VNet only.
By priority, lowest number first, until the first match. Defaults sit at the highest numbers so any explicit rule beats them. Keyword: first match.
Inbound is evaluated subnet then NIC, outbound NIC then subnet — a packet must be allowed by both. Keyword: both must permit.
Permitting a flow implicitly permits its return traffic; a reverse rule is unnecessary. Keyword: no reverse rule.
From Virtual Network Manager, evaluated before NSGs and not overridable by a subscription owner. Keyword: platform baseline.
DNAT, then network rules, then application rules. A broad network rule can pre-empt an FQDN rule. Keyword: fixed order.
Adds TLS inspection, IDPS, URL filtering, and web categories. Any inspect-inside-TLS requirement is Premium. Keyword: see inside TLS.
A central base policy extended by regional child policies, so a baseline is written once. Keyword: parent and child.
Detection first to find false positives in the logs, then prevention. Straight to prevention breaks the app. Keyword: measure then enforce.
